title: What not to put on the site for an independent school
metaTitle: What to leave off an independent school site
excerpt: Cut the mission statement in small type and the other souvenirs that delay a parent. Keep students in the day and a clear way to visit or inquire.
alt: Hands typing on a laptop at a wooden desk near a window, the edit where extra pages come off a school site.
caption: The edit happens at the keyboard. The first cut is the motto in small type. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a school site remove first?
faqs.answer: A mission statement in small type under a crest on the first screen. Parents cannot picture a Tuesday from it, and on a phone they often cannot read it. Replace it with students in a lesson, one sentence about the group, and a way to visit or inquire.

faqs.question: Which other pieces fail the same test?
faqs.answer: Crest animations, roof drones, stock children, badges you cannot explain at the gate, a stale news grid, and icon rows labeled academic and pastoral. Also remove a visit button that opens a film, and a form that asks for both parents' jobs before it offers a date.

faqs.question: What is enough to publish?
faqs.answer: A homepage with the day and a visit, ages if they differ, fees, a short about page with names, one proof of a real constraint, a contact path for exceptions, and policies in the footer. Add a term note when it is true. Anything else has to serve the day, the visit, the fee, or the exception.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Independent school website mistakes often start as things the board enjoys. The one to cut first is a mission statement in small type, usually under a crest, where a parent needed students and the day. It reassures the people who approved the wording and confuses a parent deciding where a child will spend years. Keep the day, not the emblem, and keep a clear way to visit or inquire. A shorter site that tells the truth will outperform a long site that performs taste.

Nielsen Norman Group's research explains the mechanism. Visitors often leave in 10 to 20 seconds, they read only about a quarter of the text on pages they do open, and a clear offer in the first 10 seconds is what earns any longer stay. A motto in type too small to read is not a bonus. It is a blockage in front of the two facts that would have helped. Google's people-first guidance asks a matching question: after the visit, did the person learn enough to do the thing they came to do, or do they still need to search for a Tuesday?

## Cut the mission line first

Remove the mission statement from the first screen, especially in small type under a shield. If the sentence is true, the day will show it, and a readable version can live on the about page under a name. On the homepage it does not show a child. It does not say when a parent can visit. From a phone it is often illegible, which means the layout already knew the sentence was ceremonial.

Cutting it will feel, internally, like a loss of seriousness. Sit with that feeling and do it anyway. Seriousness is not the same as information. A parent cannot award you a child because the motto was well kerned. They can visit if they understand the day.

Replace the opening with students in a real lesson, one sentence about the age and the group, and a way to visit or inquire. You have removed the most common mistake and installed the most common repair. The rest of this essay is the same test applied to everything else a committee will try to restore.

Keep the agreed sentence in the governor's handbook if they need it on paper. The site is the comparison a parent actually uses.

## What the board is protecting

Boards protect the mission line because it took a year to agree, because a predecessor wrote it, or because it sounds like the schools they admire. They protect a crest animation for the same reason. They protect an alumni paragraph because it sounds like the speeches in which the school congratulates itself.

None of these are contemptible. They are institutional souvenirs. The site is not the archive. A souvenir reassures people who already belong. A parent does not belong yet. Souvenirs read as delay, and delay reads as avoidance of the day, which is a frightening impression when the decision lasts years.

Ask, of any element people are angry to lose: does this help a stranger see the day, or book a visit, or understand the fee? If the answer is "it expresses who we are," require a second sentence that names the parent's decision. If that sentence cannot be written, the element is a souvenir. Thank it. Take it off the first screen and out of the header. You can keep it in a governor's pack.

If the new site opens on the same small mission line, the redesign only changed the type. Put the cut list in the brief, or the parent meets the old school in new colors.

## What the parent is doing

The parent is not attending your heritage. They are in a comparison. Three schools, a year group, a fee they must justify to themselves or to a partner, a child who will live inside the choice. They will give you a few seconds, then a few more if the day is intelligible. The quarter-of-the-text finding means your long page is already an unread page. Write for the quarter you will get. Delete the rest, or put it behind a click a curious person chooses.

They are also wary. They have toured places that spoke of nurture and delivered a child nobody seemed to know. Your motto triggers that memory even when your classrooms are good. Honesty is how you avoid being filed with the disappointments.

The job list is short. The day, a visit, the fee shape, the ages, a human for the exception. Anything else needs a reason tied to a real family question. "Because the page felt empty" is not a family question. Empty, on a school site, is often the feeling of a page that has become usable.

Do not add pages to chase search visits. Google's guidance is plain that people-first pages are the point, and that padding, trend-chasing, and pages that leave a reader needing another search are the failure. A short true page about a year-4 morning is better than a long page that says "excellence" and never shows a class size.

## Keep the students and the day

What stays is the day as it is. The lesson, the group, the gate, the lunch, the pickup. Captions with ages. Limits you would otherwise confess by email: the stair, the yard, the hour the day ends, the support you do not offer. If you teach three distinct stages, three true descriptions beat one blended dream. Blending is a common mistake. The best lab from the senior school, the smallest class from the nursery, a lawn from a campus you share, presented as "life at the school."

Keep the sentence that would have prevented a bad tour. The end time. The absence of a bus. The class size. The fact that a year is full. Teams cut these because they fear they will lose the family. They lose a worse thing when they keep a family and forfeit trust in the first term. The site's job is the right place, not the maximum inquiry count.

Keep photography that matches the term you are in. A permanent sports-day hero in February is a mistake even if the file is joyful. Swap it for a lesson. Do not ask a parent to imagine the Tuesday you declined to show.

If a picture exists because the lawn was pretty, and it hides a constraint you mention only on the phone, the picture is a mistake. Put that honesty on the page.

## Keep the way to visit or inquire

The second thing that stays is the path. A header label in plain words. Open mornings with real dates. A short inquiry for the family that cannot tour yet, with a reply window you keep. A fee page that states what is included. A phone layout where the control is reachable and does not jump when the picture loads.

Mistakes around this path are ordinary and serious. A "Visit" button that opens a film of the crest. A PDF prospectus as the only admissions route. A form that asks for both parents' jobs before it offers a date. A mission line restored above the button in type the board can see on a projector and a parent cannot see on a pavement.

Fix the path before you add features. A shop, a donate module, a popup for the gala, a virtual tour that starts in the chapel and skips the stair. Each one competes with the visit. On a small school the competition matters because the office is also teaching, or also the head. One path. Then exceptions.

If the visit page is clumsy and the crest page is precious, you have decorated the wrong object. Spend the care on the dates, the year groups, the confirmation, the gate. Beauty at the edge of a confusing inquiry is a classic mistake. Families remember the confusion because that is where they risked a child's years.

## Other cuts that pass the same test

Apply the souvenir test across the site. Cut a crest animation that plays before any student. Cut a drone shot of the roof. Cut stock children. Cut award badges you cannot explain in one spoken sentence at the gate. Cut a news grid you do not update, because a last post from three years ago makes a living school look asleep. Cut a page for every keyword you hope to rank for, if it repeats "nurturing" and shows no day.

Cut a virtual tour that flatters the hall and hides the stair. Cut "experiences" that are a list of trips you ran once. A short note about a trip you actually repeat is not a mistake. A fake global program is. Cut icon rows labeled academic, pastoral, and co-curricular. Cut any sentence that could move to the next school's site with the name swapped. Those sentences are the padding a parent skips on the way to a fact. Let the fact stand. It will feel bare in the committee preview and clear on the phone.

Keep policies, linked by their names: admissions, fees, safeguarding, privacy. Hiding a rule because it feels unfriendly is the mistake in the other direction. Unfriendly is a parent who could not find the end time. The rule can be firm and still be printed in normal type.

## A shorter site

When the cuts are done, the site should feel almost too small to the people who loved the prospectus. Homepage with students and a visit. The day, by age if the ages differ. Fees. A short about page with names. One proof about a real constraint. A contact path for exceptions. Policies in the footer. That is a complete school site. You can add a term note when you have something true to say. You do not add it to fill a template that expected a magazine.

Read the shorter site against the quarter-of-the-text constraint. A person who reads a quarter of a short, factual page has read the decision. A person who reads a quarter of a long, tasteful page has read an adjective and a crest. Choose the first outcome.

Then stop. The ongoing mistake is to reopen the cut list every time a vendor offers a module or a governor misses the motto. New modules must serve the day, the visit, the fee, or the exception. If they do not, they are the mission line in software form.

The same discipline changes again when the buyer is not a parent. A person deciding whether to join a club is looking for people playing and a way to see the schedule, and the souvenir in the way is often a trophy cabinet. [What a club homepage has to prove to someone deciding whether to join](/blog/what-the-homepage-has-to-prove-for-a-community-sports-club) is the next piece. The test stays strict. The object moves from the school day to the game.

When you want help holding the cut list through a redesign, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring the sentence the board is most proud of. The useful work often starts by asking whether a parent can see a child in it.
